correctness.rationale: For a plant with pollinator neighbor set N, extinction has probability q to the cardinality of N, and pairwise extinction depends only on union size. Equality of labeled first- and second-order laws therefore identifies all plant degrees and pair codegrees. With at most three plants and known pollinator degrees the incidence multiset can be recovered by inclusion–exclusion. For all at most eight-vertex connected networks, the included verifier enumerates every nonzero incidence-row tuple and computes the exact maximum-matching rank on every surviving-pollinator subset; it finds no signature with unequal profile vectors. In the nine-species witness, the identical degrees and codegrees are checked directly; the rank-profile difference is (0,0,1,3,3,0), giving exact gap \(q(1-q)^2(3-3q+q^2)\). All seven pointwise improving subsets are enumerated and the gap is positive throughout the open probability interval. Finite enumeration is used only for the explicitly bounded sharpness claim.

originality.rationale: The full Memmott–Waser–Price (2004) paper studies network-driven secondary plant extinction under removal and not maximum-matching service allocation; the full available Bock–Rautenbach (2018) article characterizes static matching-number feasibility for bipartite degree sequences and does not assert a degree-plus-pair-codegree determination theorem for the stochastic deletion rank profile. A recent claim on nine-species matching-ranking crossover in accessible prior work assumes only degree-matched graphs and its displayed witnesses have different plant pairwise codegrees. The present first/second-order coextinction-law nonidentifiability with exact nine-vertex sharpness therefore is not implied by those checked results. No matching indexed or accessible historical statement was found, while undiscovered transversal-matroid formulations remain a live risk.

value.rationale: Exact natural identifiability gap: all individual and pairwise plant-loss laws and pollinator degrees agree but one-to-one assignment service capacity is strictly ordered at seven identifiable failure outcomes. Both fully intact networks have the same maximum matching size, so the effect is not an obvious static-degree difference. The exhaustive eight-vertex cutoff is a sharp and motivated structural boundary and yields a small reproducible benchmark for distinguishing abundance-risk signatures from assignment risk. No general downstream theorem is asserted.
